41825:
Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea in the rugged highlands of Seir, its capital Bozrah, its strongholds in the rocks (Obad 1:3). Israel never forgot that Edom's ancestor was Esau, Jacob's twin. The Torah told Israel not to hate an Edomite 'for he is your brother' (Deut 23:7). Yet relations were bitter: Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness (Num 20:14-21), was conquered by David, and revolted under Jehoram.

The crisis Obadiah describes is most likely the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC. Several texts accuse Edom of joining in: Psalm 137 recalls Edomites shouting 'Tear it down!' and Lamentations and Ezekiel both name Edom (Lam 4:21-22; Ezek 35:5-15). Obadiah 1-9 closely parallels Jeremiah 49:7-22; scholars debate whether one borrowed from the other or both used an older oracle. A minority of conservative scholars date Obadiah to the 840s BC raid under Jehoram (2 Chr 21:16-17), placing it early in the Twelve; the book itself does not say.

Edom's fate in history matched the oracle's direction. After Babylon's campaigns in the 550s Edom faded; its people drifted into southern Judah (later called Idumea), and the Nabataeans built Petra in its old heartland. Ironically, Herod the Great was an Idumean.

41836:
Obadiah is the haftarah for parashat Vayishlach (Gen 32-36), where Jacob meets Esau again and Esau's descendants, the kings of Edom, are listed. The pairing makes the point: the brotherly tension of Genesis becomes a national story. The book's last line, 'and the kingdom shall be the LORD's' (Obad 1:21), is woven into Jewish liturgy, recited in the morning service's 'Song at the Sea' section and in the Rosh Hashanah kingship verses (malkhuyot).

In rabbinic literature 'Edom' became a code name for Rome, the empire that destroyed the second temple, and in the medieval period for Christendom. So Obadiah was read as a promise that the oppressive empire of the day would fall and Zion's saviours would 'judge the mount of Esau'. The Talmud's tradition that Obadiah was a convert from Edom (*Sanhedrin* 39b) makes a striking point: the prophet who condemns Edom is someone who left Edom's ways. The relational frame is constant: God is the protector of a wounded family member, and history is heading toward his kingship.

41895:
Nineveh, on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was one of Assyria's oldest and greatest cities, and from about 705 BC its capital. Assyrian kings boasted in their inscriptions of flaying rebels, impaling captives and stacking heads, and their palace reliefs (some now in the British Museum) show these scenes in stone. For Israelites, Nineveh meant the empire that destroyed Samaria and devastated Judah. When the book calls it 'that great city' it means both its size and its notoriety.

The story is set when Jonah was active under Jeroboam II, though the book was probably written later. Its form is debated. Many Christians and Jews have read it as history; Jesus refers to Jonah and the Ninevites in the same breath as the Queen of Sheba (Matt 12:41-42). Many modern scholars read it as a didactic story or prophetic parable, pointing to features such as the exaggerated size of Nineveh ('three days' journey'), the unnamed 'king of Nineveh' (Assyrian kings were called king of Assyria), animals in sackcloth, and the irony-filled plot. Both camps agree on the main thing: the book is crafted with great skill to make a theological point.

That point comes in chapter 4. Jonah fled not from fear but because he knew God was 'gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love' (Jonah 4:2), the creed of Exodus 34. He wanted justice for Nineveh, not mercy. The book ends without his answer to God's question, leaving readers to supply their own.

41907:
The whole book of Jonah is read as the haftarah at the afternoon (Minchah) service of Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year, followed by Micah 7:18-20 ('Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity'). At the climax of a day of fasting and confession, Israel hears of pagan sailors who pray, a city that repents in sackcloth, and a God who relents. The message is that teshuvah (repentance) works, that no one is beyond it, and that one cannot run from God, a theme the medieval commentators drew from Jonah's flight 'from the presence of the LORD'.

Rabbinic tradition also asked why Jonah fled. One answer (in the *Mekhilta* and later Rashi) is that Jonah feared that Nineveh's quick repentance would shame Israel, which had not repented at the words of its prophets; another is that he was protecting his own reputation as a true prophet. Midrash identifies Jonah with the son of the widow of Zarephath whom Elijah raised (Jerusalem Talmud *Sukkah* 5:1), and *Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer* expands the fish episode richly. Uriel Simon's JPS commentary sums up the Jewish reading: the book teaches that God's compassion extends to all his creatures, and that justice and mercy must be held together.

41972:
Micah's home region, the Shephelah, was Judah's breadbasket and buffer zone. It lay on the route any army from the coast would take toward Jerusalem. The towns he laments in chapter 1, with wordplays on their names (Mic 1:10-15), include Lachish, Judah's second city. In 701 BC Sennacherib took Lachish after a siege that he celebrated in huge stone reliefs for his palace at Nineveh; his annals claim he captured forty-six fortified cities of Judah. For Micah's neighbours, his warnings came true in their lifetimes.

Inside Judah the problem was land. Israel's Torah treated family land as an inheritance from God that should stay in the clan (Lev 25:23; Num 27:7-11). In Micah's day powerful people 'covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away' (Mic 2:2), turning free farmers into tenants or debt slaves. Judges, priests and prophets all worked for payment (Mic 3:11), while assuring everyone that 'the LORD is among us; no disaster will come'.

The book alternates between doom and hope three times (Mic 1-2, Mic 3-5, Mic 6-7). Scholars debate how much of the hope comes from Micah and how much from later disciples, but the structure itself makes a point: God's judgment is real, and so is his determination to gather a remnant and bring peace.

41984:
Micah's closing words are some of the most used in Jewish worship. Micah 7:18-20 ('Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity... you will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea') is read at the end of the Yom Kippur afternoon haftarah after Jonah, and on Rosh Hashanah it forms the heart of Tashlikh, the custom of going to flowing water and symbolically casting sins away. Its last verse, 'You will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love (hesed) to Abraham, as you swore to our fathers', grounds forgiveness in God's covenant loyalty to the patriarchs.

Micah 5:6-6:8 (Hebrew numbering) is the haftarah for parashat Balak, because Micah 6:5 recalls Balak and Balaam. The Talmud (*Makkot* 24a) says Micah summed up the whole Torah in three principles: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your God (Mic 6:8). In Jewish reading this verse does not replace the commandments but expresses their heart; 'walk humbly' (hatzne'a lekhet) is applied to modest, private acts of charity and to quiet faithfulness. The vision of nations streaming to Zion to learn Torah and beating swords into ploughshares (Mic 4:1-4) shapes Jewish messianic hope for a world at peace under God's instruction.
